rows.subtopic: Coulomb's Law and Forces Between Multiple Charges
rows.stem: Figure shows variation of Coulomb force (F) acting between two point charges with \(\frac{1}{r^2}\), r being the separation between the two charges \((q_1, q_2)\) and \((q_2, q_3)\). If \(q_2\) is positive and least in magnitude, then the magnitudes of \(q_1\), \(q_2\) and \(q_3\) are such that
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem says only 'Figure shows variation' and every option is an ordering of the three magnitudes, so the whole question is the geometry of the two plotted lines. Described: a graph with F on the vertical axis and \(\frac{1}{r^2}\) on the horizontal axis, carrying two straight lines through the origin, one labelled \((q_1, q_2)\) and the other labelled \((q_2, q_3)\). Deliberately WITHHELD: the sign and the relative steepness of the two slopes — slope is proportional to the product of the charges, so naming either would hand over both the sign of \(q_3\) and the ordering the options ask for. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
Coulomb's law written against the variable actually plotted is
\(F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}q_{a}q_{b}\left(\dfrac{1}{r^{2}}\right)\)
so a graph of F against \(\dfrac{1}{r^{2}}\) is a STRAIGHT LINE THROUGH THE ORIGIN whose slope is \(kq_{a}q_{b}\). Both the SIGN and the STEEPNESS of each line therefore carry information.
READING THE SIGNS. From the figure the \((q_{1}, q_{2})\) line has a POSITIVE slope, so \(q_{1}q_{2} > 0\) and those two charges have the SAME sign; the force between them is repulsive. The \((q_{2}, q_{3})\) line has a NEGATIVE slope, so \(q_{2}q_{3} < 0\) and those two have OPPOSITE signs, the force being attractive.
Since \(q_{2}\) is given as positive, it follows that \(q_{1}\) is positive and \(q_{3}\) is negative.
READING THE STEEPNESS. The magnitudes of the slopes compare the products:
\(|\text{slope}_{1}| = k|q_{1}||q_{2}| \qquad |\text{slope}_{2}| = k|q_{2}||q_{3}|\)
The \((q_{1}, q_{2})\) line is visibly the STEEPER of the two, so
\(|q_{1}||q_{2}| > |q_{2}||q_{3}| \quad\Longrightarrow\quad |q_{1}| > |q_{3}|\)
the common \(|q_{2}|\) cancelling.
Finally the stem states that \(q_{2}\) is the LEAST in magnitude. Combining:
\(q_{2} < q_{3} < q_{1}\)
The question is really two readings of one graph — sign from the direction of each line, magnitude from its steepness — and the stem supplies the third fact that anchors them.

rows.stem: Two wires P and Q are made of the same material. The wire Q has twice the diameter and half the length as that of wire P. If the resistance of wire P is R, the resistance of the wire Q will be
rows.solution:
The resistance of a wire is
\(R = \dfrac{\rho l}{A} = \dfrac{\rho l}{\pi r^{2}}\)
and both wires are of the SAME material, so \(\rho\) is common and only the geometry differs.
Wire Q has TWICE THE DIAMETER, hence twice the radius, so its area is FOUR times that of P:
\(A_{Q} = \pi(2r)^{2} = 4\pi r^{2} = 4A_{P}\)
Wire Q also has HALF THE LENGTH:
\(l_{Q} = \dfrac{l_{P}}{2}\)
Both changes push the resistance DOWN, and they multiply:
\(R_{Q} = \dfrac{\rho l_{Q}}{A_{Q}} = \dfrac{\rho\left(\dfrac{l_{P}}{2}\right)}{4A_{P}} = \dfrac{1}{8}\cdot\dfrac{\rho l_{P}}{A_{P}}\)
\(R_{Q} = \dfrac{R}{8}\)
The factor of 8 is \(2 \times 4\), and the 4 is where the question is won: doubling a DIAMETER quadruples an area, because area goes as the square of the radius. A reader who treats the diameter change as a factor of 2 arrives at \(\dfrac{R}{4}\), which is not offered, and one who uses only the length change arrives at \(\dfrac{R}{2}\), which is.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem: A 1 cm segment of a wire lying along x-axis carries current of 0.5 A along +x direction. A magnetic field \(\vec{B} = (0.4\ \text{mT})\,\hat{j} + (0.6\ \text{mT})\,\hat{k}\) is switched on, in the region. The force acting on the segment is
rows.solution:
The force on a current-carrying segment is
\(\vec{F} = I\left(\vec{L} \times \vec{B}\right)\)
The segment lies along the x-axis, so \(\vec{L} = (1\ \mathrm{cm})\hat{i} = 10^{-2}\hat{i}\ \mathrm{m}\), and with \(I = 0{\cdot}5\) A,
\(I\vec{L} = 0{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-2}\,\hat{i} = 5 \times 10^{-3}\,\hat{i}\ \mathrm{A\,m}\)
The field is \(\vec{B} = \left(0{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-3}\right)\hat{j} + \left(0{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-3}\right)\hat{k}\ \mathrm{T}\).
Take the cross product term by term, using \(\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}\) and \(\hat{i} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{j}\):
\(\vec{F} = 5 \times 10^{-3}\,\hat{i} \times \left[\left(0{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-3}\right)\hat{j} + \left(0{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-3}\right)\hat{k}\right]\)
\(\vec{F} = \left(5 \times 10^{-3}\right)\left(0{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-3}\right)\hat{k} + \left(5 \times 10^{-3}\right)\left(0{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-3}\right)\left(-\hat{j}\right)\)
\(\vec{F} = 2 \times 10^{-6}\,\hat{k} - 3 \times 10^{-6}\,\hat{j}\)
\(\vec{F} = \left(-3\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\right)\ \mu\mathrm{N}\)
Two traps sit in the options. The MINUS SIGN on \(\hat{j}\) comes from \(\hat{i} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{j}\), the one cyclic product that reverses; and the COMPONENTS SWAP, the \(\hat{j}\) component of \(\vec{B}\) producing the \(\hat{k}\) component of \(\vec{F}\) and vice versa. The two mN options are a thousand times too large, from carrying the field in millitesla without converting.

rows.stem: A coil has 100 turns, each of area 0.05 \(\mathrm{m^2}\) and total resistance 1.5 \(\Omega\). It is inserted at an instant in a magnetic field of 90 mT, with its axis parallel to the field. The charge induced in the coil at that instant is :
rows.solution:
The charge that flows through a coil while the flux changes does NOT depend on how fast the change happens.
From Faraday's law and Ohm's law together,
\(q = \int i\,dt = \int \dfrac{|\varepsilon|}{R}\,dt = \int \dfrac{N}{R}\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}\,dt = \dfrac{N\Delta\phi}{R}\)
The dt cancels, which is why the phrase "at that instant" in the stem does not need a time.
The coil is inserted with its AXIS PARALLEL to the field, so the field is perpendicular to the plane of each turn and the flux through one turn goes from 0 to its full value BA:
\(\Delta\phi = BA = \left(90 \times 10^{-3}\right)\left(0{\cdot}05\right) = 4{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{Wb}\)
Hence
\(q = \dfrac{N\Delta\phi}{R} = \dfrac{100 \times 4{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-3}}{1{\cdot}5} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}45}{1{\cdot}5}\)
\(q = 0{\cdot}30\ \mathrm{C}\)
The induced charge is 0.30 C. The distractor 0.45 C is the numerator \(N\Delta\phi\) left undivided by the resistance, and 3.0 mC is the same figure with the factor of 100 turns dropped.

rows.stem: You are required to design an air-filled solenoid of inductance 0.016 H having a length 0.81 m and radius 0.02 m. The number of turns in the solenoid should be
rows.solution:
The self-inductance of a long solenoid is
\(L = \mu_{0}n^{2}Al\)
where n is the number of turns PER UNIT LENGTH. Writing it in terms of the total number of turns N, with \(n = \dfrac{N}{l}\):
\(L = \mu_{0}\dfrac{N^{2}}{l^{2}}Al = \dfrac{\mu_{0}N^{2}A}{l} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad N = \sqrt{\dfrac{Ll}{\mu_{0}A}}\)
The cross-sectional area is
\(A = \pi r^{2} = \pi\left(0{\cdot}02\right)^{2} = 1{\cdot}257 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^{2}}\)
Substituting \(L = 0{\cdot}016\) H, \(l = 0{\cdot}81\) m and \(\mu_{0} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\):
\(N^{2} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}016 \times 0{\cdot}81}{\left(4\pi \times 10^{-7}\right)\left(1{\cdot}257 \times 10^{-3}\right)} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}296 \times 10^{-2}}{1{\cdot}579 \times 10^{-9}}\)
\(N^{2} = 8{\cdot}21 \times 10^{6}\)
\(N \approx 2866\)
About 2866 turns are needed.
The four options are close enough together that the arithmetic has to be carried honestly — they differ by only a few per cent, so an approximation anywhere will land on the wrong one. Note also that L depends on the SQUARE of N, so a 10% error in the turns count is a 20% error in the inductance.

rows.subtopic: Power in AC Circuits and the Power Factor
rows.stem: A voltage \(v = v_0 \sin \omega t\) applied to a circuit drives a current \(i = i_0 \sin (\omega t + \phi)\) in the circuit. The average power consumed in the circuit over a cycle is
rows.solution:
The instantaneous power is the product of the instantaneous voltage and current:
\(P = vi = \left(v_{0}\sin\omega t\right)\left[i_{0}\sin(\omega t + \phi)\right]\)
Expanding the second sine, \(\sin(\omega t + \phi) = \sin\omega t\cos\phi + \cos\omega t\sin\phi\):
\(P = i_{0}v_{0}\left[\sin^{2}\omega t\cos\phi + \sin\omega t\cos\omega t\sin\phi\right]\)
Now average over a complete cycle, and take the two terms separately.
The first carries \(\sin^{2}\omega t\), whose average over a cycle is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) — the square is never negative, so it cannot average to zero.
The second carries \(\sin\omega t\cos\omega t = \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2\omega t\), a pure sinusoid whose average over a cycle IS zero.
So only the first survives:
\(P_{av} = i_{0}v_{0}\cos\phi \times \dfrac{1}{2}\)
\(P_{av} = \dfrac{i_{0}v_{0}}{2}\cos\phi\)
Equivalently \(P_{av} = V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi\), the factor \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) being the two factors of \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) combined.
The option \(\dfrac{i_{0}v_{0}}{2}\) is what a purely resistive circuit gives, where \(\phi = 0\); \(i_{0}v_{0}\cos\phi\) has lost the cycle-average of \(\sin^{2}\); and "zero" is true only for a purely reactive circuit, where \(\phi = 90^{\circ}\).

rows.stem: The given diagram exhibits the relationship between the wavelength of the electromagnetic waves and the energy of photon associated with them. The three points P, Q and R marked on the diagram may correspond respectively to :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — every option is an ordering of three named radiations against the marked points, so the answer is entirely in where P, Q and R sit on the curve. Described: a graph with Energy on the vertical axis and Wavelength (marked \(\lambda\)) on the horizontal axis, carrying a single smooth curve that falls steeply and then flattens towards the right, with three points labelled P, Q and R marked on it. Deliberately WITHHELD: the order in which P, Q and R appear along that curve, which is exactly the discrimination the four options test. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
The two axes are related by
\(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\)
so energy varies INVERSELY with wavelength, which is why the plotted curve falls steeply and then flattens rather than being a straight line. Reading off the three marked points:
P sits HIGH on the curve and far to the LEFT — the shortest wavelength, the highest photon energy.
R sits in the MIDDLE, at intermediate wavelength and energy.
Q sits far to the RIGHT and LOW — the longest wavelength, the lowest photon energy.
Now place the three named radiations on the electromagnetic spectrum. Of X-rays, ultraviolet and microwaves, X-rays have much the shortest wavelength (about 1 nm down to \(10^{-3}\) nm), ultraviolet is intermediate (400 nm to 1 nm), and microwaves are much the longest (0.1 m to 1 mm).
Matching them to the positions:
P = X-rays, Q = microwaves, R = UV radiation.
The order the question asks for is P, Q, R — not the order in which the points appear along the curve — so the answer reads X-rays, microwaves, UV radiation. Two of the distractors are the same three radiations in spectrum order, which is what a reader produces by answering the question that was not asked.

rows.stem: A beaker is filled with water (refractive index \(\frac{4}{3}\)) upto a height H. A coin is placed at its bottom. The depth of the coin, when viewed along the near normal direction, will be
rows.solution:
When an object under water is viewed from almost directly above, refraction at the surface makes it appear NEARER than it is. The relation between the two depths is
\(\mu = \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}\)
The coin's real depth is the full height of the water, H, so
\(\text{apparent depth} = \dfrac{H}{\mu} = \dfrac{H}{\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)} = \dfrac{3H}{4}\)
The coin appears to be at a depth of \(\dfrac{3H}{4}\).
The direction of the shift is worth fixing firmly: since \(\mu > 1\) for water, the apparent depth is always LESS than the real depth — the bottom of a pool always looks closer than it is, never further. The option \(\dfrac{4H}{3}\) is the same arithmetic with the ratio inverted, and it describes a physical situation that does not occur.
The phrase "along the near normal direction" matters because the simple ratio holds only for rays close to the vertical; viewed obliquely the apparent position shifts sideways too, and the formula no longer applies.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem: The stopping potential \(V_0\) measured in a photoelectric experiment for a metal surface is plotted against frequency \(\nu\) of the incident radiation. Let m be the slope of the straight line so obtained. Then the value of charge of an electron is given by (h is the Planck's constant.)
rows.solution:
Einstein's photoelectric equation, written for the stopping potential, is
\(eV_{0} = h\nu - \phi_{0}\)
Rearranging into the form of a straight line, with \(V_{0}\) as the y variable and \(\nu\) as the x variable:
\(V_{0} = \left(\dfrac{h}{e}\right)\nu - \dfrac{\phi_{0}}{e}\)
Comparing with \(y = mx + c\), the slope of the graph is
\(m = \dfrac{h}{e}\)
Solving for the electronic charge:
\(e = \dfrac{h}{m}\)
This is not merely an algebraic exercise. The slope depends ONLY on \(\dfrac{h}{e}\) and on nothing about the metal — the work function appears solely in the INTERCEPT. So every metal gives a line of the SAME slope, and a different intercept; it was exactly this universality that Millikan's measurements confirmed, and it is how h was first determined photoelectrically once e was known.
The distractor mh inverts the relation, and \(\dfrac{m}{h}\) gives \(\dfrac{1}{e}\) rather than e.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.stem: Let \(\lambda_e\), \(\lambda_p\) and \(\lambda_d\) be the wavelengths associated with an electron, a proton and a deuteron, all moving with the same speed. Then the correct relation between them is
rows.solution:
The de Broglie wavelength is
\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{mv}\)
All three particles move with the SAME speed, so v cancels out of any comparison and
\(\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{m}\)
The LIGHTEST particle therefore has the LONGEST wavelength.
Ordering the masses: an electron is about 1/1836 of a proton, and a deuteron is a proton plus a neutron, so roughly twice a proton:
\(m_{e} \ll m_{p} < m_{d}\)
Inverting the order:
\(\lambda_{e} > \lambda_{p} > \lambda_{d}\)
The gap is enormously lopsided, which is worth noticing: \(\lambda_{e}\) exceeds \(\lambda_{p}\) by a factor of about 1836, while \(\lambda_{p}\) exceeds \(\lambda_{d}\) by only about 2. It is precisely because the electron's mass is so small that its wave nature is observable at laboratory energies, and why electron diffraction was demonstrated long before neutron diffraction.
The option \(\lambda_{e} = \lambda_{p} = \lambda_{d}\) would require the wavelength to depend on speed alone, ignoring the mass in the momentum.

rows.stem: Which of the following figures correctly represent the shape of curve of binding energy per nucleon as a function of mass number ?

options.label: A
options.text: a plot of \(\frac{\mathrm{B.E.}}{\mathrm{A}}\) against A that rises steeply from a low value, reaches a broad flat maximum just past the dashed vertical line marked 56, and then falls away slowly

options.label: B
options.text: a plot of \(\frac{\mathrm{B.E.}}{\mathrm{A}}\) against A that rises steeply and levels off at the dashed vertical line marked 56, remaining almost flat for the whole of the rest of the range

options.label: C
options.text: a plot of \(\frac{\mathrm{B.E.}}{\mathrm{A}}\) against A that begins low and flat, rises to an almost symmetric hump peaking at the dashed vertical line marked 80, and then falls back to a low flat value

options.label: D
options.text: a plot of \(\frac{\mathrm{B.E.}}{\mathrm{A}}\) against A that rises steeply to a peak at the dashed vertical line marked 80, falls to a shallow minimum and then turns upward again at the far right

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the four options ARE four drawn graphs and the printed paper gives them no text at all. The option texts above are a plain reading of what each graph draws (axis labels, the dashed tick value, the shape); they are lossless, and picking between them still requires knowing the real binding-energy curve, so nothing is handed over. Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
The binding-energy-per-nucleon curve has a characteristic shape, and each feature of it carries physics.
It RISES STEEPLY for small mass numbers, because a nucleon in a very light nucleus has few neighbours to bind to, and each nucleon added brings a disproportionate gain.
It reaches a BROAD, FLAT MAXIMUM of about 8.5 MeV per nucleon in the region around \(A \approx 56\), the iron-nickel region. The flatness is the SATURATION of the short-range nuclear force: beyond a certain size a nucleon interacts only with its immediate neighbours, so its share of the binding stops growing.
It then FALLS AWAY SLOWLY for heavy nuclei, because the long-range Coulomb repulsion between protons grows as \(Z^{2}\) and increasingly offsets the nuclear attraction.
So the correct figure is the one that rises steeply, tops out in a broad flat maximum just past \(A = 56\), and then declines gently.
The three wrong shapes each fail on one of those features. One levels off at 56 and stays flat, which would leave no energy to be released by fission. One shows a symmetric hump peaking at 80, which puts the maximum in the wrong place. One turns upward again at the far right, which would make the heaviest nuclei the most tightly bound of all — the opposite of what makes uranium fissionable.
Both fusion and fission are read off this curve: light nuclei move towards the peak by FUSING, heavy ones by SPLITTING, and each moves to a higher binding energy per nucleon, releasing the difference.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem: When a p-n junction diode is forward biased

options.label: A
options.text: the barrier height and the depletion layer width both increase.

options.label: B
options.text: the barrier height increases and the depletion layer width decreases.

options.label: C
options.text: the barrier height and the depletion layer width both decrease.

options.label: D
options.text: the barrier height decreases and the depletion layer width increases.

rows.solution:
In forward bias the external voltage is applied so as to OPPOSE the junction's built-in field: the positive terminal goes to the p-side and the negative terminal to the n-side.
THE BARRIER HEIGHT. The applied voltage acts against the built-in potential \(V_{0}\), so the effective barrier drops to
\(V_{0} - V\)
and the barrier height DECREASES.
THE DEPLETION WIDTH. The two are not independent. The depletion region exists because diffusing carriers left immobile ions behind; weakening the field lets majority carriers push back INTO the junction region, where they neutralise some of those ions. Fewer uncovered ions means a NARROWER depletion layer.
So in forward bias the barrier height and the depletion layer width BOTH DECREASE.
They always move together, which is what disposes of the two options pairing an increase with a decrease: both are measures of the same thing, the amount of uncovered fixed charge at the junction. Increase one and you increase the other.
This is also why forward current rises so steeply: a lower barrier means exponentially more majority carriers have enough thermal energy to cross it. Reverse bias does the exact opposite, raising the barrier and widening the layer.

rows.subtopic: Lenz's Law and Conservation of Energy
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : It is difficult to move a magnet into a coil of large number of turns when the circuit of the coil is closed.
Reason (R) : The direction of induced current in a coil with its circuit closed, due to motion of a magnet, is such that it opposes the cause.
rows.context: Note : Question numbers 13 to 16 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given – one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

rows.solution:
Both statements are TRUE, and the reason is the correct explanation.
The REASON is Lenz's law, and it is correct: the induced current opposes the change that produced it. As the magnet approaches the coil, the induced current circulates so as to present a LIKE POLE to the approaching magnet, which repels it.
The ASSERTION follows directly. To keep pushing the magnet in, the experimenter must work AGAINST that repulsion, so the magnet is difficult to move. The circuit must be CLOSED for this to happen, which is why the assertion says so: with the circuit open an emf is still induced but no current flows, there is no opposing force, and the magnet moves freely.
The phrase "large number of turns" is what makes the effect pronounced. The induced emf is proportional to N, and the current it drives produces a field proportional to N again, so the opposing force grows roughly as \(N^{2}\).
Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. The energy bookkeeping is the deeper point: the extra work done against the repulsion is exactly the energy dissipated as \(i^{2}R\) heat in the coil. If the induced current ATTRACTED the magnet instead, the magnet would accelerate inward while also generating heat, creating energy from nothing.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The deflection in a galvanometer is directly proportional to the current passing through it.
Reason (R) : The coil of a galvanometer is suspended in a uniform radial magnetic field.
rows.context: Note : Question numbers 13 to 16 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given – one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

rows.solution:
Both statements are TRUE, and the reason is the correct explanation.
In a moving-coil galvanometer the deflecting torque on the coil is
\(\tau = NIAB\sin\theta\)
where \(\theta\) is the angle between the field and the plane's normal. The restoring torque of the suspension is \(k\varphi\), so at equilibrium
\(NIAB\sin\theta = k\varphi \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \varphi = \dfrac{NAB\sin\theta}{k}\,I\)
For the deflection \(\varphi\) to be DIRECTLY PROPORTIONAL to I, everything multiplying I must be CONSTANT as the coil turns — and \(\sin\theta\) is the problem, since \(\theta\) changes as the coil deflects.
This is exactly what the RADIAL field fixes. The pole pieces are made concave and a soft-iron cylinder is placed inside the coil, so the field lines are radial: wherever the coil comes to rest, its plane is always PARALLEL to the local field, making \(\theta = 90^{\circ}\) and \(\sin\theta = 1\) at every position. Hence
\(\varphi = \left(\dfrac{NAB}{k}\right)I \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \varphi \propto I\)
Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Without the radial field the scale would be crowded at one end and stretched at the other; with it, the divisions are uniform and the instrument can be read linearly.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : We cannot form a p-n junction diode by taking a slab of a p-type semiconductor and physically joining it to another slab of a n-type semiconductor.
Reason (R) : In a p-type semiconductor \(\eta_e \gg \eta_h\) while in a n-type semiconductor \(\eta_h \gg \eta_e\).
rows.context: Note : Question numbers 13 to 16 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given – one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

rows.solution:
The ASSERTION is TRUE. Simply pressing a slab of p-type material against a slab of n-type does NOT make a p-n junction. On the scale that matters — a few hundred atomic spacings — the two surfaces touch only at scattered high points, leaving gaps far wider than the depletion region needs to be. There is no continuous crystal lattice across the boundary, so the diffusion and drift that create a depletion layer cannot take place. A real junction is grown as ONE single crystal, doped p-type on one side and n-type on the other, so the lattice runs unbroken through the junction.
The REASON is FALSE, and it has the two carrier types the wrong way round. In a p-type semiconductor the dopant is trivalent and HOLES are the majority carriers, so \(n_{h} \gg n_{e}\). In an n-type semiconductor the dopant is pentavalent and ELECTRONS are the majority carriers, so \(n_{e} \gg n_{h}\). The reason states the exact opposite of both.
So the assertion is true but the reason is false.
Even had the reason been stated correctly it would not have explained the assertion, since the obstacle to joining two slabs is the discontinuity of the CRYSTAL LATTICE, not the carrier concentrations — which are, after all, exactly what a genuine junction has on its two sides.

Assertion (A) : The potential energy of an electron revolving in any stationary orbit in a hydrogen atom is positive.
Reason (R) : The total energy of a charged particle is always positive.
