rows.solution:
Both statements are FALSE.
The ASSERTION is false. The electron and the nucleus carry opposite charges, so their electrostatic potential energy is NEGATIVE:
\(U = \dfrac{(+e)(-e)}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r} = -\dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r}\)
taking U as zero when the two are infinitely far apart. The negative sign says work must be done to pull them apart, which is what being bound means. The potential energy of an orbiting electron is negative, not positive.
The REASON is false as stated in even broader terms. There is no rule that the total energy of a charged particle is always positive. A free electron far from anything has positive kinetic energy and zero potential energy, so its total is positive; but an electron BOUND in an atom has total energy
\(E = K + U = -\dfrac{e^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_{0}r}\)
which is negative. The sign is not a property of the charge at all — it depends on the ZERO chosen for the potential energy and on whether the particle is bound.
So the assertion is false and the reason is also false. The negative total energy is the defining signature of a bound state, in atoms as in planetary orbits, and for hydrogen it is what gives the familiar \(E_{n} = -\dfrac{13{\cdot}6}{n^{2}}\) eV.

rows.stem: A battery of emf E and internal resistance r is connected to a rheostat. When a current of 2A is dawn from the battery, the potential difference across the rheostat is 5V. The potential difference becomes 4V when a current of 4A is drawn from the battery. Calculate the value of E and r.
rows.solution:
The terminal potential difference of a cell delivering current I is
\(V = E - Ir \quad\Longrightarrow\quad E = V + Ir\)
and the rheostat is the external resistance, so the potential difference across it IS the terminal voltage.
Each observation gives one equation.
FIRST CASE, \(I = 2\) A and \(V = 5\) V:
\(E = 5 + 2r \qquad \ldots(1)\)
SECOND CASE, \(I = 4\) A and \(V = 4\) V:
\(E = 4 + 4r \qquad \ldots(2)\)
Two equations, two unknowns. Equating them:
\(5 + 2r = 4 + 4r\)
\(1 = 2r \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r = 0{\cdot}5\ \Omega\)
Substituting back into (1):
\(E = 5 + 2(0{\cdot}5)\)
\(E = 6\ \mathrm{V}\)
The emf is 6 V and the internal resistance \(0{\cdot}5\ \Omega\).
The pattern is worth keeping: drawing MORE current from a cell always LOWERS its terminal voltage, and here doubling the current from 2 A to 4 A dropped it from 5 V to 4 V. The size of that drop is what measures r — a cell whose terminal voltage barely sags under load has a small internal resistance.

rows.stem: In a diffraction experiment, the slit is illuminated by light of wavelength 600 nm. The first minimum of the pattern falls at \(\theta = 30^\circ\). Calculate the width of the slit.
rows.solution:
For single-slit diffraction the MINIMA occur where
\(a\sin\theta = n\lambda \qquad (n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots)\)
It is worth being clear why this is the condition for DARKNESS rather than brightness. Divide the slit into two halves; when the path difference between the two EDGES of the slit is \(n\lambda\), every point in the first half has a partner in the second half exactly half a wavelength out of step, so the contributions cancel in pairs and the resultant is zero.
For the FIRST minimum, \(n = 1\):
\(a\sin 30^{\circ} = \lambda\)
\(a \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 600 \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}\)
\(a = 1200 \times 10^{-9}\)
\(a = 1{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}\)
The slit is \(1{\cdot}2\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) wide.
Note how narrow that is — only twice the wavelength of the light used. That is exactly what a first minimum as far out as \(30^{\circ}\) implies: diffraction spreads light appreciably only when the aperture is comparable to the wavelength, and a slit even ten times wider would place its first minimum below \(3^{\circ}\).

rows.stem: In a Young's double-slit experiment, two light waves, each of intensity \(\mathrm{I_o}\), interfere at a point, having a path difference \(\frac{\lambda}{8}\) on the screen. Find the intensity at this point.
rows.solution:
Convert the path difference into a phase difference first, since the intensity formula is written in terms of phase:
\(\Delta\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \times \Delta x = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \times \dfrac{\lambda}{8}\)
\(\Delta\phi = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\)
For two waves of intensity \(I_{0}\) each,
\(I = I_{0} + I_{0} + 2\sqrt{I_{0}I_{0}}\cos\Delta\phi = 2I_{0}\left(1 + \cos\Delta\phi\right)\)
Substituting \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\):
\(I = 2I_{0}\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = 2I_{0} + \sqrt{2}I_{0}\)
\(I = \left(2 + \sqrt{2}\right)I_{0} \approx 3{\cdot}414\,I_{0}\)
The equivalent form \(I = 4I_{0}\cos^{2}\dfrac{\Delta\phi}{2} = 4I_{0}\cos^{2}\dfrac{\pi}{8}\) gives the same number.
The result sits sensibly between the two extremes the pattern allows: \(4I_{0}\) at a bright fringe and 0 at a dark one. An eighth of a wavelength is a small path difference, so the point is much nearer a maximum than a minimum — and note that \(3{\cdot}414\,I_{0}\) is well above the \(2I_{0}\) the two beams would give with no interference at all.

rows.stem: A transparent solid cylindrical rod (refractive index \(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\)) is kept in air. A ray of light incident on its face travels along the surface of the rod, as shown in figure. Calculate the angle \(\theta\).
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem names \(\theta\) only as 'the angle' and points at the drawing for what it is measured from. Described: a horizontal cylindrical rod drawn in perspective with its axis marked by a dashed line, and a ray arriving from the lower left, striking the flat circular end face and continuing to the right along the curved surface of the rod, with the angle \(\theta\) marked at the point of incidence. Deliberately WITHHELD: which line \(\theta\) is measured against (the axis or the normal to the end face), since that choice is what turns the total-internal-reflection condition into a number. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
The ray is described as travelling ALONG the surface of the rod after refraction, which is the defining condition for the critical angle: a ray that grazes the boundary is one striking it at exactly \(\theta_{c}\).
STEP 1 — THE CRITICAL ANGLE at the curved surface, going from glass into air:
\(\sin\theta_{c} = \dfrac{n_{1}}{n_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\right)} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\)
\(\theta_{c} = 60^{\circ}\)
STEP 2 — THE ANGLE OF REFRACTION AT THE FLAT FACE. Inside the rod, the ray refracted at the flat end face and the ray striking the curved surface are the SAME ray, and the two normals concerned — one along the rod's axis, one perpendicular to its side — are at right angles. So the two angles are complementary:
\(r = 90^{\circ} - \theta_{c} = 90^{\circ} - 60^{\circ} = 30^{\circ}\)
STEP 3 — SNELL'S LAW AT THE FLAT FACE, where the ray enters from air:
\(n_{1}\sin\theta = n_{2}\sin r\)
\(1 \times \sin\theta = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \times \sin 30^{\circ} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \times \dfrac{1}{2}\)
\(\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\)
\(\theta = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \approx 35^{\circ}\)
The complementary step is the one that carries the whole question: nothing in the stem states the angle at the curved wall, and it has to be got from the geometry of two perpendicular normals. This is also the calculation behind an optical fibre's acceptance angle — any ray entering at less than \(\theta\) strikes the wall beyond the critical angle and is trapped inside, and \(\theta\) is the largest angle for which that still works.

rows.subtopic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem: Prove that, in Bohr model of hydrogen atom, the time period of revolution of an electron in \(n^{\mathrm{th}}\) orbit is proportional to \(n^3\).
rows.solution:
The period is the time to go once round the orbit:
\(T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} \qquad \ldots(1)\)
so the n-dependence of T follows from those of r and v.
THE SPEED. From Bohr's quantisation of angular momentum,
\(mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi mr} \qquad \ldots(2)\)
Substituting (2) into (1):
\(T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{\left(\dfrac{nh}{2\pi mr}\right)} = \dfrac{4\pi^{2}mr^{2}}{nh}\)
THE RADIUS. Bohr's model gives the orbit radius as
\(r = \dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}}{4\pi^{2}mke^{2}}\)
so \(r \propto n^{2}\) and hence \(r^{2} \propto n^{4}\). Substituting:
\(T = \dfrac{4\pi^{2}m}{nh}\left(\dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}}{4\pi^{2}mke^{2}}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{n^{3}h^{3}}{4\pi^{2}mk^{2}e^{4}}\)
\(T \propto n^{3}\)
which is what was to be proved.
The short route is to track the two dependencies separately. Since \(r \propto n^{2}\) and, from (2) with \(r \propto n^{2}\), \(v \propto \dfrac{n}{r} \propto \dfrac{1}{n}\), equation (1) gives
\(T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} \propto \dfrac{n^{2}}{\left(\dfrac{1}{n}\right)} = n^{3}\)
Both factors push the same way: outer orbits are both LONGER round and traversed more SLOWLY, so the period grows faster than the size. The \(n^{3}\) law is the atomic counterpart of Kepler's third law, which it resembles for exactly the same reason — both describe motion under an inverse-square attraction.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.stem: A p-type Si semiconductor is made by doping an average of one dopant atom per \(5 \times 10^7\) silicon atoms. If the number density of silicon atoms in the specimen is \(5 \times 10^{28}\) atoms \(\mathrm{m^{-3}}\), find the number of holes created per cubic centimetre in the specimen due to doping. Also give one example of such dopants.
rows.solution:
Each dopant atom in a p-type semiconductor is TRIVALENT. It forms only three covalent bonds with its four silicon neighbours, leaving the fourth bond incomplete — and that incomplete bond IS a hole. So the count is one hole per dopant atom, and the arithmetic is just the doping ratio.
HOLES PER CUBIC METRE:
\(n_{h} = \dfrac{\text{number density of Si atoms}}{\text{Si atoms per dopant atom}} = \dfrac{5 \times 10^{28}}{5 \times 10^{7}}\)
\(n_{h} = 10^{21}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}\)
CONVERTING TO PER CUBIC CENTIMETRE. Since \(1\ \mathrm{m^{3}} = 10^{6}\ \mathrm{cm^{3}}\), divide by \(10^{6}\):
\(n_{h} = \dfrac{10^{21}}{10^{6}}\)
\(n_{h} = 10^{15}\ \mathrm{holes\ per\ cm^{3}}\)
EXAMPLE OF SUCH A DOPANT: aluminium (indium and gallium serve equally well — any trivalent, Group 13 element).
The cube in the unit conversion is the step to watch: a metre is \(10^{2}\) cm, so a cubic metre is \(10^{6}\) cubic centimetres, not \(10^{2}\).
It is worth noting how small the doping is — one atom in fifty million — and yet \(10^{15}\) holes per cm³ utterly dominates the intrinsic carrier concentration of silicon, which is only about \(10^{10}\) per cm³ at room temperature. That five-order-of-magnitude gap is why a trace impurity controls the conductivity completely.

rows.stem:
Two batteries of emf's 3V & 6V and internal resistances 0.2 \(\Omega\) & 0.4 \(\Omega\) are connected in parallel. This combination is connected to a 4 \(\Omega\) resistor. Find :
(i) the equivalent emf of the combination
(ii) the equivalent internal resistance of the combination
(iii) the current drawn from the combination
rows.solution:
(i) EQUIVALENT EMF.
For two cells in parallel the equivalent emf is a weighted average in which each emf is weighted by the OTHER cell's internal resistance:
\(E_{eq} = \dfrac{E_{1}r_{2} + E_{2}r_{1}}{r_{1} + r_{2}}\)
Substituting \(E_{1} = 3\) V with \(r_{1} = 0{\cdot}2\ \Omega\), and \(E_{2} = 6\) V with \(r_{2} = 0{\cdot}4\ \Omega\):
\(E_{eq} = \dfrac{3 \times 0{\cdot}4 + 6 \times 0{\cdot}2}{0{\cdot}2 + 0{\cdot}4} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}2 + 1{\cdot}2}{0{\cdot}6} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}4}{0{\cdot}6}\)
\(E_{eq} = 4\ \mathrm{V}\)
(ii) EQUIVALENT INTERNAL RESISTANCE — the two internal resistances in parallel:
\(r_{eq} = \dfrac{r_{1}r_{2}}{r_{1} + r_{2}} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}2 \times 0{\cdot}4}{0{\cdot}6} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}08}{0{\cdot}6}\)
\(r_{eq} = 0{\cdot}133\ \Omega\)
(iii) CURRENT DRAWN. The combination now behaves as a single 4 V cell of internal resistance \(0{\cdot}133\ \Omega\) driving the \(4\ \Omega\) resistor:
\(I = \dfrac{E_{eq}}{R + r_{eq}} = \dfrac{4}{4 + 0{\cdot}133} = \dfrac{4}{4{\cdot}133}\)
\(I \approx 0{\cdot}97\ \mathrm{A}\)
(the marking scheme rounds this to 0.9 A).
Two features of the answer are worth noting. The equivalent emf, 4 V, lies between the two emfs but NOT midway — it is much closer to 3 V, because the 3 V cell has the SMALLER internal resistance and therefore the greater say. And \(r_{eq}\) is smaller than either internal resistance, which is the practical reason for putting cells in parallel: the combination can supply more current than either cell alone.

rows.stem:
(i) A conductor of length \(l\) is connected across an ideal cell of emf E. Keeping the cell connected, the length of the conductor is increased to \(2l\) by gradually stretching it. If R and \(\mathrm{R}'\) are initial and final values of resistance and \(v_d\) and \(v_d'\) are initial and final values of drift velocity, find the relation between (i) \(\mathrm{R}'\) and R and (ii) \(v_d'\) and \(v_d\).
(ii) When electrons drift in a conductor from lower to higher potential, does it mean that all the 'free electrons' of the conductor are moving in the same direction ?
rows.solution:
(i) STRETCHING THE CONDUCTOR.
The key physical fact is that stretching does not change the amount of METAL, only its shape. The volume is conserved:
\(Al = A'l' \quad\text{with}\quad l' = 2l\)
\(Al = A'(2l) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad A' = \dfrac{A}{2}\)
So doubling the length HALVES the cross-section.
RELATION BETWEEN \(R'\) AND R:
\(R = \dfrac{\rho l}{A} \qquad R' = \dfrac{\rho l'}{A'} = \dfrac{\rho(2l)}{\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)} = 4\dfrac{\rho l}{A}\)
\(R' = 4R\)
Both changes raise the resistance, and they multiply — which is why stretching a wire to n times its length multiplies its resistance by \(n^{2}\), not by n.
RELATION BETWEEN \(v_{d}'\) AND \(v_{d}\). The cell stays connected, so the potential difference V across the conductor is UNCHANGED. The field inside is \(E = \dfrac{V}{l}\), and
\(v_{d} = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m} = \dfrac{eV\tau}{ml}\)
The length is the only thing in this that changed, and it doubled:
\(\dfrac{v_{d}'}{v_{d}} = \dfrac{l}{l'} = \dfrac{1}{2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v_{d}' = \dfrac{v_{d}}{2}\)
Note that the AREA does not enter here at all: the drift velocity is set by the field, and the field is set by the voltage and the length alone.
(ii) NO. The free electrons are not all moving in the same direction.
At any instant the electrons are in rapid RANDOM thermal motion, at speeds of the order of \(10^{5}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), colliding constantly with the lattice ions and scattering in every direction. The applied field superimposes on this chaos a very small systematic DRIFT — of the order of \(10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), a billion times smaller.
So what moves uniformly is the AVERAGE, not the individuals. Drift velocity is the mean of a vast number of randomly directed velocities that very nearly, but not quite, cancel; at any given moment a great many electrons are travelling the "wrong" way.

rows.subtopic: Biot-Savart Law and Field of a Circular Loop
rows.stem: Using Biot-Savart law, derive expression for the magnetic field \((\vec{B})\) due to a circular current carrying loop at a point on its axis and hence at its centre.
rows.solution:
FIELD AT A POINT ON THE AXIS.
Let a circular loop of radius R carry current I, and let P lie on the axis at distance x from the centre O.
Take a current element \(Id\vec{l}\) on the loop. Its distance to P is
\(r = \sqrt{R^{2} + x^{2}}\)
and because the element lies in the plane of the loop while the line to P runs from the rim to the axis, \(d\vec{l}\) is PERPENDICULAR to \(\vec{r}\) for every element. So the Biot-Savart law,
\(dB = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^{2}}\)
takes \(\sin\theta = 1\) throughout, giving
\(dB = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl}{\left(R^{2} + x^{2}\right)}\)
THE SYMMETRY ARGUMENT, which is the heart of the derivation. The field \(d\vec{B}\) is perpendicular to both \(d\vec{l}\) and \(\vec{r}\), so it is tilted with respect to the axis. Resolve it into a component ALONG the axis, \(dB\cos\alpha\), and one PERPENDICULAR to it. Now consider the diametrically opposite element: its perpendicular component points exactly the other way. Taking the loop in such pairs, ALL the perpendicular components cancel and only the axial ones survive.
From the geometry \(\cos\alpha = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{R^{2} + x^{2}}}\), so
\(B = \oint dB\cos\alpha = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi\left(R^{2} + x^{2}\right)} \times \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{R^{2} + x^{2}}}\oint dl\)
The remaining integral is just the circumference, \(\oint dl = 2\pi R\):
\(B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi} \times \dfrac{R \times 2\pi R}{\left(R^{2} + x^{2}\right)^{3/2}}\)
\(B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}IR^{2}}{2\left(R^{2} + x^{2}\right)^{3/2}}\)
directed along the axis, its sense given by the right-hand rule.
FIELD AT THE CENTRE. Put \(x = 0\):
\(B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}IR^{2}}{2\left(R^{2}\right)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}IR^{2}}{2R^{3}}\)
\(B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I}{2R}\)
Far away, where \(x \gg R\), the expression becomes \(B \approx \dfrac{\mu_{0}IR^{2}}{2x^{3}} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{2M}{x^{3}}\) with \(M = I\pi R^{2}\) — the field of a magnetic DIPOLE on its axis. A current loop seen from a distance is indistinguishable from a small bar magnet, and this is the calculation that says so.

rows.stem:
(a) Show that the energy required to build up the current I in a coil of inductance L is \(\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{LI}^2\).
(b) Considering the case of magnetic field produced by air-filled current carrying solenoid, show that the magnetic energy density of a magnetic field B is \(\frac{\mathrm{B}^2}{2\mu_0}\).
rows.solution:
(a) ENERGY STORED IN AN INDUCTOR.
While the current in a coil is growing, the coil induces a back emf that OPPOSES the growth:
\(|\varepsilon| = L\dfrac{dI}{dt}\)
The source must therefore do work against this back emf, and that work is what gets stored. The rate of doing it at any instant is
\(\dfrac{dW}{dt} = |\varepsilon|I = LI\dfrac{dI}{dt}\)
so the work done while the current rises by dI is \(dW = LI\,dI\). Integrating from zero to the final current I:
\(W = \int_{0}^{I} LI\,dI = L\left[\dfrac{I^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{I}\)
\(W = \dfrac{1}{2}LI^{2}\)
which is the energy required to build up the current — and which is returned to the circuit when the current is switched off.
(b) ENERGY DENSITY OF A MAGNETIC FIELD.
Apply the result to a long air-filled solenoid, whose field and inductance are both known:
\(B = \mu_{0}nI \quad\Longrightarrow\quad I = \dfrac{B}{\mu_{0}n} \qquad\text{and}\qquad L = \mu_{0}n^{2}Al\)
Substituting both into the energy expression:
\(U_{B} = \dfrac{1}{2}LI^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\mu_{0}n^{2}Al\right)\left(\dfrac{B}{\mu_{0}n}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\mu_{0}n^{2}Al\right)\dfrac{B^{2}}{\mu_{0}^{2}n^{2}}\)
The \(n^{2}\) cancels and one power of \(\mu_{0}\) survives in the denominator:
\(U_{B} = \dfrac{B^{2}Al}{2\mu_{0}}\)
The field of a long solenoid is confined to its interior, of volume \(Al\), so dividing by that volume gives the energy per unit volume:
\(u_{B} = \dfrac{U_{B}}{Al}\)
\(u_{B} = \dfrac{B^{2}}{2\mu_{0}}\)
Every property of the particular solenoid — n, A and l — has cancelled, leaving an expression in B alone. That is what justifies calling it a property of the FIELD rather than of the coil, and the same energy density applies to any magnetic field however produced. It is the exact magnetic counterpart of the electric energy density \(\dfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_{0}E^{2}\), and the two together carry the energy of an electromagnetic wave.

rows.stem:
(a) A parallel plate capacitor is charged by an ac source. Show that the sum of conduction current \((\mathrm{I_c})\) and the displacement current \((\mathrm{I_d})\) has the same value at all points of the circuit.
(b) In case (a) above, is Kirchhoff's first rule (junction rule) valid at each plate of the capacitor ? Explain.
rows.solution:
(a) THE SUM \(I_{c} + I_{d}\) IS THE SAME EVERYWHERE.
The problem Maxwell faced is that a capacitor BREAKS the conducting path: charge flows in the wires but nothing crosses the gap between the plates. The resolution is that a changing electric field in the gap constitutes a current of its own.
OUTSIDE THE CAPACITOR, in the connecting wires, there is a real flow of charge but no changing electric flux, so
\(I_{d} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad I_{c} + I_{d} = I_{c} = I\)
INSIDE THE CAPACITOR, between the plates, no charge crosses, so \(I_{c} = 0\) and only the displacement current remains:
\(I_{c} + I_{d} = I_{d} = \varepsilon_{0}\dfrac{d\phi_{E}}{dt}\)
Now evaluate that. The field between the plates is uniform, \(E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_{0}} = \dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_{0}A}\), so the flux through the gap is
\(\phi_{E} = EA = \dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_{0}}\)
and therefore
\(I_{d} = \varepsilon_{0}\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_{0}}\right) = \dfrac{dQ}{dt}\)
But \(\dfrac{dQ}{dt}\) is exactly the rate at which charge arrives along the wire, which is \(I_{c}\). So
\(I_{d}\ \text{(inside)} = I_{c}\ \text{(outside)}\)
Hence \(I_{c} + I_{d}\) has the SAME value at every point of the circuit — \(I_{c}\) in the wires, an equal \(I_{d}\) in the gap.
(b) YES, Kirchhoff's junction rule remains valid at each plate.
Treat a capacitor plate as a junction. Conduction current \(I_{c}\) arrives along the wire; displacement current \(I_{d}\) leaves through the gap. Since
\(I_{c} = I_{d}\)
what enters equals what leaves, and the junction rule holds exactly.
This is precisely why the displacement current had to be introduced. Without it, applying Ampere's law to two different surfaces bounded by the same loop — one cutting the wire, one passing between the plates — would give two different answers, and current would appear to vanish at the plate. The displacement term restores the continuity of current, and with it the junction rule, everywhere.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Photoelectric Effect and its Experimental Study
rows.stem:
Answer the following giving reason :
(a) All the photo electrons do not eject with the same kinetic energy when monochromatic light is incident on a metal surface.
(b) The saturation current in case (a) is different for different intensity.
(c) If one goes on increasing the wavelength of light incident on a metal surface, keeping its intensity constant, emission of photo electrons stop at a certain wavelength for this metal.
rows.solution:
(a) WHY THE PHOTOELECTRONS HAVE A RANGE OF KINETIC ENERGIES.
Every photon in a monochromatic beam carries the SAME energy \(h\nu\), but the electrons do not all start from the same depth. Einstein's equation
\(K_{max} = h\nu - \phi_{0}\)
gives the MAXIMUM kinetic energy, and the work function \(\phi_{0}\) is the MINIMUM energy needed — it applies to the most loosely bound electrons, those right at the surface.
Electrons lying deeper in the metal are more tightly bound, and they lose further energy in collisions on their way out. Each such electron therefore emerges with LESS than \(K_{max}\). The result is a continuous spread of kinetic energies from zero up to \(K_{max}\), even though the incident light is of a single frequency.
(b) WHY THE SATURATION CURRENT DEPENDS ON INTENSITY.
The saturation current is reached when EVERY emitted photoelectron is collected, so it measures the NUMBER of electrons emitted per second and nothing else.
One photon can liberate at most one electron, so the number of electrons per second is proportional to the number of PHOTONS arriving per second. At a fixed frequency each photon carries the same energy, so the number arriving per second is proportional to the intensity. Hence
\(I_{saturation} \propto \text{intensity}\)
Note the division of labour that runs through the whole phenomenon: intensity controls HOW MANY electrons come out, frequency controls HOW ENERGETIC each one is. Neither crosses over into the other's role.
(c) WHY EMISSION STOPS BEYOND A CERTAIN WAVELENGTH.
As the wavelength increases the frequency falls, and with it the energy of each photon:
\(E = h\nu = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\)
Emission requires a single photon to supply at least the work function on its own, since two photons essentially never arrive at one electron together. So emission continues only while
\(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} \geq \phi_{0} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda \leq \lambda_{0} = \dfrac{hc}{\phi_{0}}\)
Beyond this THRESHOLD WAVELENGTH \(\lambda_{0}\) every photon is individually too feeble, and emission ceases abruptly.
Holding the intensity constant is what makes this decisive. It means energy still arrives at the same rate — indeed MORE photons arrive per second, each being weaker — and yet nothing at all is emitted. That is the observation classical wave theory could not survive, since on a wave picture the electron should simply absorb energy for longer until it had enough.

rows.stem:
(a) Define 'Mass defect' and 'Binding energy' of a nucleus. Describe 'Fission process' on the basis of binding energy per nucleon.
(b) A deuteron contains a proton and a neutron and has a mass of 2.013553 u. Calculate the mass defect for it in u and its energy equivalence in MeV. \((\mathrm{m_p} = 1.007277\ \mathrm{u},\ \mathrm{m_n} = 1.008665\ \mathrm{u},\ 1\mathrm{u} = 931.5\ \mathrm{MeV/c^2})\)
rows.solution:
(a) DEFINITIONS AND THE FISSION PROCESS.
MASS DEFECT is the difference between the sum of the masses of a nucleus's constituent nucleons taken separately and the actual mass of the nucleus:
\(\Delta m = \left[Zm_{p} + (A - Z)m_{n}\right] - M_{nucleus}\)
The nucleus is always LIGHTER than its parts.
BINDING ENERGY is the energy equivalent of that missing mass, \(E_{b} = \Delta m\,c^{2}\) — the energy that would have to be supplied to separate the nucleus completely into its individual nucleons, or equivalently the energy released when they came together.
FISSION ON THE BASIS OF BINDING ENERGY PER NUCLEON. The binding-energy-per-nucleon curve peaks at about 8.5 MeV near \(A \approx 56\) and DECLINES for heavier nuclei, so a very heavy nucleus such as uranium (\(A \approx 235\), about 7.6 MeV per nucleon) is LESS tightly bound per nucleon than the medium-mass nuclei it can break into (about 8.5 MeV per nucleon).
When such a heavy nucleus splits into two lighter fragments, every one of its nucleons moves to a more tightly bound state. The binding energy per nucleon INCREASES by roughly 0.9 MeV, and with about 235 nucleons involved the total energy released is of the order of 200 MeV per fission.
(b) MASS DEFECT AND ENERGY OF THE DEUTERON.
A deuteron is one proton plus one neutron, so
\(\Delta m = \left(m_{p} + m_{n}\right) - m_{d}\)
\(\Delta m = \left(1{\cdot}007277 + 1{\cdot}008665\right) - 2{\cdot}013553\)
\(\Delta m = 2{\cdot}015942 - 2{\cdot}013553\)
\(\Delta m = 0{\cdot}002389\ \mathrm{u}\)
Converting with \(1\ \mathrm{u} = 931{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^{2}\):
\(E_{b} = 0{\cdot}002389 \times 931{\cdot}5\)
\(E_{b} \approx 2{\cdot}22\ \mathrm{MeV}\)
Carry all six decimal places through the subtraction — the two totals agree to two decimal places, so rounding the input masses destroys the answer entirely.
That 2.22 MeV is the binding energy of the WHOLE deuteron, so its binding energy per nucleon is only about 1.11 MeV — far below the 8.5 MeV plateau. The deuteron is the most weakly bound stable nucleus there is, which is why deuterium is so readily consumed in fusion.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem:
(a) Draw circuit arrangement for studying V-I characteristics of a p-n junction diode.
(b) Show the shape of the characteristics of a diode.
(c) Mention two information that you can get from these characteristics.
rows.solution:
(a) CIRCUIT ARRANGEMENT.
TWO separate circuits are needed, because the two halves of the characteristic differ by orders of magnitude in current.
FOR FORWARD BIAS: connect the battery's positive terminal to the p-side of the diode through a rheostat, a VOLTMETER across the diode, and a MILLIAMMETER in series to read the current. Forward currents run to tens of milliamperes.
FOR REVERSE BIAS: reverse the battery so the positive terminal goes to the n-side, and replace the milliammeter with a MICROAMMETER. Reverse currents are only a few microamperes, and a milliammeter would show nothing at all.
Label the diode's p and n ends, the voltmeter, the ammeter, the rheostat and the switch in both diagrams.
(b) SHAPE OF THE CHARACTERISTICS.
Plot current against voltage with the origin at the centre, using DIFFERENT SCALES on the two halves — mA and volts in the first quadrant, \(\mu\)A and volts in the third.
FORWARD (first quadrant): the current stays almost zero until the KNEE VOLTAGE — about 0.7 V for silicon, 0.3 V for germanium — after which it rises very steeply and nearly vertically.
REVERSE (third quadrant): a tiny, almost constant reverse saturation current of a few \(\mu\)A, flat over a wide range of voltage, until the BREAKDOWN VOLTAGE is reached, where the current increases sharply in magnitude.
(c) TWO PIECES OF INFORMATION OBTAINABLE:
THE KNEE (CUT-IN) VOLTAGE, read off as the forward voltage at which the current begins to rise steeply — it identifies the semiconductor material.
THE BREAKDOWN VOLTAGE, the reverse voltage at which the reverse current suddenly rises — it sets the maximum reverse voltage the diode can safely withstand.
(Either of these may be replaced by the reverse saturation current, or by the observation that the diode has a very low resistance in forward bias and a very high one in reverse — which is the asymmetry that makes rectification possible.)

rows.stem: The final charge on the capacitor, when key \(\mathrm{S_1}\) is closed and \(\mathrm{S_2}\) is open, is
rows.context:
A circuit consisting of a capacitor C, a resistor of resistance R and an ideal battery of emf V, as shown in figure is known as RC series circuit.
As soon as the circuit is completed by closing key \(\mathrm{S_1}\) (keeping \(\mathrm{S_2}\) open) charges begin to flow between the capacitor plates and the battery terminals. The charge on the capacitor increases and consequently the potential difference \(V_c\) (= q/C) across the capacitor also increases with time. When this potential difference equals the potential difference across the battery, the capacitor is fully charged (Q = VC). During this process of charging, the charge q on the capacitor changes with time t as
\(q = Q[1 - e^{-t/RC}]\)
The charging current can be obtained by differentiating it and using \(\frac{d}{dx}(e^{mx}) = m e^{mx}\).
Consider the case when R = 20 k\(\Omega\), C = 500 \(\mu\)F and V = 10 V.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the passage says 'as shown in figure' and never states how the two keys sit in the circuit, which is what every sub-part turns on. Described: a rectangular loop carrying, on its upper arm, a capacitor labelled C; on its left arm, a resistor drawn as a zig-zag and labelled R; on its lower arm, a battery labelled V; and, in the middle of the loop, two switches drawn one above the other and labelled \(\mathrm{S_2}\) (upper) and \(\mathrm{S_1}\) (lower), each connecting the left branch to the right branch. Deliberately WITHHELD: which of the two branches each key completes, i.e. which one puts the battery in the loop and which one shorts it out — that is precisely the discrimination between sub-parts (i) and (ii). Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
The passage supplies the charging law
\(q = Q\left[1 - e^{-t/RC}\right]\)
and the question asks for the FINAL charge, that is the value as \(t \to \infty\). The exponential then vanishes and the bracket tends to 1, so the final charge is simply Q — which the passage identifies as
\(Q = VC\)
With the stated values \(V = 10\) V and \(C = 500\ \mu\mathrm{F}\):
\(Q = 10 \times 500 \times 10^{-6}\)
\(Q = 5 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{C} = 5\ \mathrm{mC}\)
The final charge is 5 mC.
The resistance does not appear, and that is worth noticing. R controls only HOW FAST the capacitor charges, through the time constant RC; it has no influence on the final charge, which is fixed by the battery voltage and the capacitance alone. A larger R simply means a longer wait for the same 5 mC.
The distractor \(5\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) is the same figure with the microfarad prefix mishandled, and 0.1 C comes from dividing by C rather than multiplying.

rows.stem: For sufficient time the key \(\mathrm{S_1}\) is closed and \(\mathrm{S_2}\) is open. Now key \(\mathrm{S_2}\) is closed and \(\mathrm{S_1}\) is open. What is the final charge on the capacitor ?
rows.context:
A circuit consisting of a capacitor C, a resistor of resistance R and an ideal battery of emf V, as shown in figure is known as RC series circuit.
As soon as the circuit is completed by closing key \(\mathrm{S_1}\) (keeping \(\mathrm{S_2}\) open) charges begin to flow between the capacitor plates and the battery terminals. The charge on the capacitor increases and consequently the potential difference \(V_c\) (= q/C) across the capacitor also increases with time. When this potential difference equals the potential difference across the battery, the capacitor is fully charged (Q = VC). During this process of charging, the charge q on the capacitor changes with time t as
\(q = Q[1 - e^{-t/RC}]\)
The charging current can be obtained by differentiating it and using \(\frac{d}{dx}(e^{mx}) = m e^{mx}\).
Consider the case when R = 20 k\(\Omega\), C = 500 \(\mu\)F and V = 10 V.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — same shared circuit as sub-part (i), and this sub-part is entirely about what closing \(\mathrm{S_2}\) instead of \(\mathrm{S_1}\) does to the loop, which the passage never states. Described and withheld exactly as on Q29(i). Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
Read what the switching does. With \(\mathrm{S_{1}}\) OPEN the battery is disconnected from the loop entirely, and with \(\mathrm{S_{2}}\) CLOSED the charged capacitor is connected across the resistor R alone.
That is a DISCHARGING circuit. With no source to maintain it, the capacitor drives its own charge round through R, where it is dissipated as heat, and the charge decays as
\(q = Q\,e^{-t/RC}\)
Asked for the FINAL charge, take \(t \to \infty\): the exponential tends to zero and so does q.
The final charge on the capacitor is ZERO.
The decay is asymptotic rather than abrupt — after one time constant about 37% remains, after five about 0.7% — but it has no non-zero limit, because there is nothing in the loop to stop the process until the last of the charge has gone.
The distractor 5 mC is the charge the capacitor started with, correct for the previous sub-part and for the instant before \(\mathrm{S_{2}}\) closes; 2.5 mC would be right if the charge merely halved, which is what would happen if it were shared with a second, equal capacitor rather than discharged through a resistor.

rows.stem: The dimensional formula for RC is
rows.context:
A circuit consisting of a capacitor C, a resistor of resistance R and an ideal battery of emf V, as shown in figure is known as RC series circuit.
As soon as the circuit is completed by closing key \(\mathrm{S_1}\) (keeping \(\mathrm{S_2}\) open) charges begin to flow between the capacitor plates and the battery terminals. The charge on the capacitor increases and consequently the potential difference \(V_c\) (= q/C) across the capacitor also increases with time. When this potential difference equals the potential difference across the battery, the capacitor is fully charged (Q = VC). During this process of charging, the charge q on the capacitor changes with time t as
\(q = Q[1 - e^{-t/RC}]\)
The charging current can be obtained by differentiating it and using \(\frac{d}{dx}(e^{mx}) = m e^{mx}\).
Consider the case when R = 20 k\(\Omega\), C = 500 \(\mu\)F and V = 10 V.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — this is the ONE sibling of the five that is answerable with no reference to the drawing at all: it is pure dimensional analysis of the product RC, and R and C are both named in the passage. The shared circuit is still worth showing beside it so the case study reads as one thing, but it carries no data this sub-part needs. Same drawing as Q29(i). Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
The exponent in \(e^{-t/RC}\) must be a pure number, since one cannot raise e to a quantity carrying units. Therefore \(\dfrac{t}{RC}\) is dimensionless, which means RC has the SAME dimensions as time:
\(\left[RC\right] = \left[T\right] = \left[\mathrm{M^{0}\,L^{0}\,T\,A^{0}}\right]\)
The dimensional formula is \(\left[\mathrm{M^{0}\,L^{0}\,T\,A^{0}}\right]\).
The same answer follows the long way, by multiplying the two dimensional formulae out. Resistance is \(\left[\mathrm{M\,L^{2}\,T^{-3}\,A^{-2}}\right]\) and capacitance is \(\left[\mathrm{M^{-1}\,L^{-2}\,T^{4}\,A^{2}}\right]\), and their product leaves every dimension cancelling except a single power of T. Both of those appear among the options on their own, offered to a reader who supplies one factor and forgets the other.
This is why RC is called the TIME CONSTANT of the circuit. It is the time in which the charge rises to \(\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{e}\right) \approx 63\%\) of its final value, or falls to \(\dfrac{1}{e} \approx 37\%\) on discharge — a single number characterising the speed of the whole transient. For this circuit \(RC = 20 \times 10^{3} \times 500 \times 10^{-6} = 10\) s.

rows.stem: The key \(\mathrm{S_1}\) is closed and \(\mathrm{S_2}\) is open. The value of current in the resistor after 5 seconds, is
rows.context:
A circuit consisting of a capacitor C, a resistor of resistance R and an ideal battery of emf V, as shown in figure is known as RC series circuit.
As soon as the circuit is completed by closing key \(\mathrm{S_1}\) (keeping \(\mathrm{S_2}\) open) charges begin to flow between the capacitor plates and the battery terminals. The charge on the capacitor increases and consequently the potential difference \(V_c\) (= q/C) across the capacitor also increases with time. When this potential difference equals the potential difference across the battery, the capacitor is fully charged (Q = VC). During this process of charging, the charge q on the capacitor changes with time t as
\(q = Q[1 - e^{-t/RC}]\)
The charging current can be obtained by differentiating it and using \(\frac{d}{dx}(e^{mx}) = m e^{mx}\).
Consider the case when R = 20 k\(\Omega\), C = 500 \(\mu\)F and V = 10 V.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — same shared circuit as sub-part (i); the sub-part depends on \(\mathrm{S_1}\) putting the battery into the loop through R, which only the drawing states. Described and withheld exactly as on Q29(i). Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
[CBSE graced this part: the scheme records that one mark may be given to every candidate who attempted the other parts of the question. The grace is NOT because the printed answer is wrong — the working below reaches the keyed value exactly, from the figures printed in the passage.]
The charging current is obtained by differentiating the charge:
\(i = \dfrac{dq}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt}\left[Q\left(1 - e^{-t/RC}\right)\right] = \dfrac{Q}{RC}e^{-t/RC}\)
and since \(Q = VC\), the leading factor is \(\dfrac{VC}{RC} = \dfrac{V}{R}\), which is simply the initial current \(I_{0}\):
\(i = I_{0}\,e^{-t/RC} \qquad\text{with}\qquad I_{0} = \dfrac{V}{R}\)
THE TIME CONSTANT, from the values given in the passage:
\(RC = \left(20 \times 10^{3}\right)\left(500 \times 10^{-6}\right) = 10\ \mathrm{s}\)
THE INITIAL CURRENT:
\(I_{0} = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{10}{20 \times 10^{3}} = 0{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A} = 0{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{mA}\)
AT \(t = 5\) s, which is HALF the time constant:
\(i = 0{\cdot}5\,e^{-5/10} = 0{\cdot}5\,e^{-1/2}\)
\(i = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{e}}\ \mathrm{mA}\)
The current after 5 seconds is \(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{e}}\) mA, about 0.30 mA.
The square root is where the answer is decided: at half a time constant the exponent is \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\), giving \(\sqrt{e}\) rather than e. The option \(\dfrac{1}{2e}\) is what a full time constant would give, and \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{e}}\) has lost the factor of \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) from the initial current.

rows.stem: The key \(\mathrm{S_1}\) is closed and \(\mathrm{S_2}\) is open. The initial value of charging current in the resistor, is
rows.context:
A circuit consisting of a capacitor C, a resistor of resistance R and an ideal battery of emf V, as shown in figure is known as RC series circuit.
As soon as the circuit is completed by closing key \(\mathrm{S_1}\) (keeping \(\mathrm{S_2}\) open) charges begin to flow between the capacitor plates and the battery terminals. The charge on the capacitor increases and consequently the potential difference \(V_c\) (= q/C) across the capacitor also increases with time. When this potential difference equals the potential difference across the battery, the capacitor is fully charged (Q = VC). During this process of charging, the charge q on the capacitor changes with time t as
\(q = Q[1 - e^{-t/RC}]\)
The charging current can be obtained by differentiating it and using \(\frac{d}{dx}(e^{mx}) = m e^{mx}\).
Consider the case when R = 20 k\(\Omega\), C = 500 \(\mu\)F and V = 10 V.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — same shared circuit as sub-part (i); the sub-part depends on \(\mathrm{S_1}\) putting the battery into the loop through R, which only the drawing states. Described and withheld exactly as on Q29(i). Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
At the very instant the circuit is completed the capacitor is UNCHARGED, so the potential difference across it is zero and it offers no opposition at all. The whole of the battery's emf therefore appears across the resistor, and the current takes its largest value.
Formally, from \(i = \dfrac{V}{R}e^{-t/RC}\) at \(t = 0\) the exponential is 1, leaving
\(I_{0} = \dfrac{V}{R}\)
With the values given in the passage, \(V = 10\) V and \(R = 20\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\):
\(I_{0} = \dfrac{10}{20 \times 10^{3}} = 0{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A}\)
\(I_{0} = 0{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{mA}\)
The initial charging current is 0.5 mA.
The capacitance does not enter, which is the point: at \(t = 0\) an uncharged capacitor behaves exactly like a plain WIRE, and the current is set by the resistor alone. At the other extreme, once fully charged, it behaves like a BREAK in the circuit and the current is zero. C governs only how long the journey between those two states takes.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem:
Consider the arrangement shown in figure. A black vertical arrow and a horizontal thick line with a ball are painted on a glass plate. It serves as the object. When the plate is illuminated, its real image is formed on the screen.
Which of the following correctly represents the image formed on the screen ?
rows.context: A thin lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces, at least one of which should be spherical. Applying the formula for image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a lens, one can obtain the 'lens maker formula' and then the 'lens formula'. A lens has two foci – called 'first focal point' and 'second focal point' of the lens, one on each side.

options.label: A
options.text: a vertical arrow pointing UP, crossed by an oblique line that rises to the right, with the ball at the UPPER-RIGHT end of that oblique line

options.label: B
options.text: a vertical arrow pointing UP, crossed by an oblique line that rises to the right, with the ball at the LOWER-LEFT end of that oblique line

options.label: C
options.text: a vertical arrow pointing DOWN, crossed by an oblique line that rises to the right, with the ball at the LOWER-LEFT end of that oblique line

options.label: D
options.text: a vertical arrow pointing DOWN, crossed by an oblique line that rises to the right, with the ball at the UPPER-RIGHT end of that oblique line

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — TWO drawings back this row and neither is optional. (1) The apparatus, page idx 16: an optical bench drawn in perspective with a graduated scale, carrying, from left to right, a ruled Screen, a Convex Lens in a holder, and a Light Box with Plate, with a callout labelled 'Plate on Hidden Side of Box' showing the painted plate itself. (2) The four option drawings, page idx 18, whose content is read out in the option texts above. Deliberately WITHHELD: the ORIENTATION of the arrow and the SIDE the ball sits on in the callout — the image is the object rotated through 180 degrees, so stating the object's orientation names the answer outright. The option texts are safe to read out because all four are drawn alternatives and the discrimination between them lives in the withheld object, not in them.
rows.solution:
The image formed on a SCREEN is a real image, and a real image formed by a convex lens is INVERTED. Inversion here means a rotation of the whole figure through \(180^{\circ}\) about the principal axis — not a mirror reflection, which is a different operation and would give a different answer.
Apply that rotation to each painted mark in turn.
THE VERTICAL ARROW, pointing UP on the object, is turned through \(180^{\circ}\) and so points DOWN in the image.
THE OBLIQUE LINE keeps its direction of slope. Rotating a line through \(180^{\circ}\) maps it onto a line of the SAME gradient, so a line rising to the right still rises to the right. What the rotation does change is which END is which.
THE BALL, painted at the UPPER-RIGHT end of that line on the object, is carried to the diametrically opposite end and therefore appears at the LOWER-LEFT of the line in the image.
So the image is a vertical arrow pointing DOWN, crossed by an oblique line that rises to the right, with the ball at the LOWER-LEFT end.
The oblique line is the discriminator the question is built around. The arrow alone rules out only the two "arrow up" options; it takes the ball's position to separate the remaining pair, and that turns on recognising that inversion swaps the ends of the line while preserving its slope. A reader who pictures the image as a mirror image rather than a rotation flips the slope instead, and lands on neither.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: Which of the following statements is incorrect ?
rows.context: A thin lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces, at least one of which should be spherical. Applying the formula for image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a lens, one can obtain the 'lens maker formula' and then the 'lens formula'. A lens has two foci – called 'first focal point' and 'second focal point' of the lens, one on each side.

options.label: A
options.text: For a convex mirror magnification is always negative.

options.label: B
options.text: For all virtual images formed by a mirror magnification is positive.

options.label: C
options.text: For a concave lens magnification is always positive.

options.label: D
options.text: For real and inverted images, magnification is always negative.

rows.solution:
Check each statement against the sign convention, in which the magnification is
\(m = \dfrac{h'}{h} = -\dfrac{v}{u} \quad\text{(mirror)} \qquad m = \dfrac{v}{u} \quad\text{(lens)}\)
with a POSITIVE m meaning an erect image and a NEGATIVE m an inverted one.
A CONVEX MIRROR always forms a virtual, ERECT, diminished image of a real object, whatever the object distance. An erect image has a POSITIVE magnification. So the statement that a convex mirror's magnification is always negative is INCORRECT — it is always positive.
The other three are all correct.
Virtual images formed by a MIRROR are always erect, so their magnification is positive.
A CONCAVE LENS, like a convex mirror, always gives a virtual erect diminished image of a real object, so its magnification is always positive.
And a real inverted image has, by the definition above, a negative magnification.
So the incorrect statement is the one about the convex mirror.
The unifying rule behind three of the four is worth holding: for these simple cases, VIRTUAL goes with ERECT and positive m, while REAL goes with INVERTED and negative m. The convex mirror and the concave lens are the two elements that can only ever produce the first kind, which is precisely why both are used where an upright, wide-angle view is wanted.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: A convex lens of focal length 'f' is cut into two equal parts perpendicular to the principal axis. The focal length of each part will be :
rows.context: A thin lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces, at least one of which should be spherical. Applying the formula for image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a lens, one can obtain the 'lens maker formula' and then the 'lens formula'. A lens has two foci – called 'first focal point' and 'second focal point' of the lens, one on each side.
rows.solution:
The cut is made PERPENDICULAR to the principal axis, so the lens is sliced across its thickness. Each half keeps ONE of the original curved surfaces and acquires a FLAT face where the cut was made — each piece is a plano-convex lens.
Apply the lens maker's formula. For the original biconvex lens, with radii \(R_{1} = +R\) and \(R_{2} = -R\):
\(\dfrac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left[\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{-R}\right] = (n - 1)\dfrac{2}{R}\)
For one half, with a curved face of radius R and a flat face for which \(R = \infty\) and \(\dfrac{1}{R} = 0\):
\(\dfrac{1}{f'} = (n - 1)\left[\dfrac{1}{R} - 0\right] = (n - 1)\dfrac{1}{R}\)
Comparing the two, the second bracket is HALF the first:
\(\dfrac{1}{f'} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{f}\right) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad f' = 2f\)
The focal length of each part is 2f.
The direction of the change is worth checking against intuition: losing one refracting surface means the lens bends light LESS, so it is a weaker converger and its focal length must go UP. The answer \(\dfrac{f}{2}\) is the reflex response — half a lens, half the focal length — and it gets the direction exactly backwards.
Note also that this is quite different from cutting the lens ALONG the axis, which leaves each half with BOTH curved surfaces intact and therefore with the focal length unchanged at f.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: If an object in case (i) above is 20 cm from the lens and the screen is 50 cm away from the object, the focal length of the lens used is
rows.context: A thin lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces, at least one of which should be spherical. Applying the formula for image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a lens, one can obtain the 'lens maker formula' and then the 'lens formula'. A lens has two foci – called 'first focal point' and 'second focal point' of the lens, one on each side.
rows.solution:
Read the geometry carefully: the 50 cm is measured from the OBJECT to the screen, not from the lens. The lens sits 20 cm from the object, so the image distance is the remainder:
\(v = 50 - 20 = 30\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Now apply the lens formula with the sign convention. The object is real and in front of the lens, so \(u = -20\) cm; the real image is on the far side, so \(v = +30\) cm:
\(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{30} - \dfrac{1}{(-20)} = \dfrac{1}{30} + \dfrac{1}{20}\)
Over the common denominator 60:
\(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{2 + 3}{60} = \dfrac{5}{60} = \dfrac{1}{12}\)
\(f = 12\ \mathrm{cm}\)
The focal length is 12 cm.
The subtraction at the start is the whole question. Taking the 50 cm as the image distance gives \(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{50} + \dfrac{1}{20}\) and a focal length of about 14.3 cm, which is not offered; the distractors 10 cm and 20 cm are round numbers near the correct one, so the arithmetic has to be done rather than estimated.
As a check, the image is farther from the lens than the object, so the image should be magnified: \(m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{30}{-20} = -1{\cdot}5\), real, inverted and half as large again.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: The distance of an object from first focal point of a biconvex lens is \(\mathrm{X_1}\) and distance of the image from second focal point is \(\mathrm{X_2}\). The focal length of the lens is
rows.context: A thin lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces, at least one of which should be spherical. Applying the formula for image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a lens, one can obtain the 'lens maker formula' and then the 'lens formula'. A lens has two foci – called 'first focal point' and 'second focal point' of the lens, one on each side.
rows.solution:
The distances here are measured from the FOCAL POINTS, not from the lens, which is what makes this Newton's form of the lens equation rather than the usual one.
Let the lens have focal length f, with the object at distance \(X_{1}\) beyond the first focal point and the image at \(X_{2}\) beyond the second. Measuring from the lens itself,
\(u = -\left(f + X_{1}\right) \qquad v = f + X_{2}\)
Substituting into the lens formula \(\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\):
\(\dfrac{1}{f + X_{2}} + \dfrac{1}{f + X_{1}} = \dfrac{1}{f}\)
Combining the left side over a common denominator:
\(\dfrac{\left(f + X_{1}\right) + \left(f + X_{2}\right)}{\left(f + X_{1}\right)\left(f + X_{2}\right)} = \dfrac{1}{f}\)
Cross-multiplying:
\(f\left(2f + X_{1} + X_{2}\right) = f^{2} + fX_{1} + fX_{2} + X_{1}X_{2}\)
\(2f^{2} + fX_{1} + fX_{2} = f^{2} + fX_{1} + fX_{2} + X_{1}X_{2}\)
The terms \(fX_{1}\) and \(fX_{2}\) cancel from both sides, leaving
\(f^{2} = X_{1}X_{2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad f = \sqrt{X_{1}X_{2}}\)
The focal length is the GEOMETRIC MEAN of the two distances.
The form of the answer can be checked without the algebra. The two X's are lengths, so their product is an area and only its square root can be a length — which disposes of \(X_{1}X_{2}\) at once, and of \(\sqrt{\dfrac{X_{2}}{X_{1}}}\), a pure number. \(\sqrt{X_{1} + X_{2}}\) has dimensions of the square root of a length, so it fails too. Only the geometric mean survives a dimensional check.

rows.subtopic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges
rows.stem:
(i) Two point charges 5 \(\mu\)C and \(-1\) \(\mu\)C are placed at points \((-3\ \text{cm}, 0, 0)\) and \((3\ \text{cm}, 0, 0)\) respectively. An external electric field \(\vec{E} = \frac{A}{r^2}\hat{r}\) where \(A = 3 \times 10^5\) Vm is switched on in the region. Calculate the change in electrostatic energy of the system due to the electric field.
(ii) A system of two conductors is placed in air and they have net charge of \(+80\mu\)C and \(-80\mu\)C which causes a potential difference of 16 V between them.
(1) Find the capacitance of the system.
(2) If the air between the capacitor is replaced by a dielectric medium of dielectric constant 3, what will be the potential difference between the two conductors ?
(3) If the charges on two conductors are changed to \(+160\) \(\mu\)C and \(-160\) \(\mu\)C, will the capacitance of the system change ? Give reason for your answer.
rows.solution:
(i) CHANGE IN ELECTROSTATIC ENERGY.
The question asks only for the CHANGE caused by switching on the external field, so the mutual energy of the two charges — which is unaffected by the field — will cancel and need never be computed.
Before the field is switched on:
\(U_{i} = \dfrac{kq_{1}q_{2}}{r_{12}}\)
After it is switched on, each charge additionally acquires energy in the external potential:
\(U_{f} = \dfrac{kq_{1}q_{2}}{r_{12}} + q_{1}V\left(\vec{r_{1}}\right) + q_{2}V\left(\vec{r_{2}}\right)\)
So the mutual term drops out of the difference:
\(\Delta U = q_{1}V\left(\vec{r_{1}}\right) + q_{2}V\left(\vec{r_{2}}\right)\)
THE EXTERNAL POTENTIAL. Given \(\vec{E} = \dfrac{A}{r^{2}}\hat{r}\), integrating \(dV = -\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r}\) gives
\(V = \dfrac{A}{r} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{5}}{r}\)
Both charges lie 3 cm from the origin — one at \(x = -3\) cm and the other at \(x = +3\) cm — so both sit at \(r = 3 \times 10^{-2}\) m and both see the SAME potential:
\(V = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{5}}{3 \times 10^{-2}} = 10^{7}\ \mathrm{V}\)
Hence
\(\Delta U = \left(5 \times 10^{-6}\right)\left(10^{7}\right) + \left(-1 \times 10^{-6}\right)\left(10^{7}\right) = 50 - 10\)
\(\Delta U = 40\ \mathrm{J}\)
The two contributions partly cancel because the charges are of opposite sign while the potential is the same at both — so it is the NET charge, \(+4\ \mu\mathrm{C}\), that does the work here.
(ii) (1) CAPACITANCE OF THE SYSTEM.
\(C = \dfrac{Q}{V} = \dfrac{80\ \mu\mathrm{C}}{16\ \mathrm{V}}\)
\(C = 5\ \mu\mathrm{F}\)
(2) POTENTIAL DIFFERENCE AFTER INSERTING THE DIELECTRIC.
Introducing a dielectric of constant \(K = 3\) multiplies the capacitance:
\(C' = KC = 3 \times 5 = 15\ \mu\mathrm{F}\)
The CHARGE is unchanged — the conductors were given \(\pm 80\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) and nothing has been connected to alter that — so
\(V' = \dfrac{Q}{C'} = \dfrac{80\ \mu\mathrm{C}}{15\ \mu\mathrm{F}}\)
\(V' = 5{\cdot}33\ \mathrm{V}\)
The potential difference falls by the factor K, from 16 V to 5.33 V, because the polarised dielectric sets up a field opposing the original one and so reduces the work needed to carry a charge between the conductors.
(3) NO, the capacitance does not depend on the charge given to the conductors.
Capacitance is fixed by the GEOMETRY of the system — the size, shape and separation of the conductors — and by the medium between them. Doubling the charge doubles the potential difference in exact proportion, so the RATIO \(\dfrac{Q}{V}\) is unchanged. That is precisely why capacitance is a useful quantity to define at all.

rows.stem:
(i) Consider three metal spherical shells A, B and C, each of radius R. Each shell is having a concentric metal ball of radius R/10. The spherical shells A, B and C are given charges \(+6q\), \(-4q\), and \(14q\) respectively. Their inner metal balls are also given charges \(-2q\), \(+8q\) and \(-10q\) respectively. Compare the magnitude of the electric fields due to shells A, B and C at a distance 3R from their centres.
(ii) A charge \(-6\) \(\mu\)C is placed at the centre B of a semicircle of radius 5 cm, as shown in the figure. An equal and opposite charge is placed at point D at a distance of 10 cm from B. A charge \(+5\) \(\mu\)C is moved from point 'C' to point 'A' along the circumference. Calculate the work done on the charge.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — sub-part (ii) says 'as shown in the figure' and the stem never says where C and A lie, which is the whole of the potential difference the work done depends on. Described: a horizontal straight line carrying four labelled points, in the printed left-to-right order D, C, B, A, with a semicircular arc drawn above the line from C round to A; the charge \(+6q\) is marked at D and the charge \(-6q\) is marked at B. Deliberately WITHHELD: the spacings between the four points as drawn. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
(i) COMPARING THE FIELDS AT 3R.
The point in question lies at 3R from the centre, which is OUTSIDE every shell — the shells have radius R and the inner balls only \(\dfrac{R}{10}\). For any spherically symmetric distribution, Gauss's law says the field outside depends solely on the TOTAL charge enclosed, and not at all on how that charge is arranged within.
So add up each arrangement's total charge:
SHELL A: \(+6q\) on the shell and \(-2q\) on its ball, giving \(+4q\).
SHELL B: \(-4q\) on the shell and \(+8q\) on its ball, giving \(+4q\).
SHELL C: \(+14q\) on the shell and \(-10q\) on its ball, giving \(+4q\).
All three totals are the SAME. Hence at \(r = 3R\)
\(E = \dfrac{kQ_{total}}{r^{2}} = \dfrac{k(4q)}{(3R)^{2}} = \dfrac{4kq}{9R^{2}}\)
in every case, so
\(E_{A} = E_{B} = E_{C}\)
The three arrangements are indistinguishable from outside. From 3R away, a shell carrying \(+14q\) around a ball carrying \(-10q\) is exactly as good as one carrying \(+6q\) around \(-2q\) — an external measurement can determine only the total.
(ii) WORK DONE IN MOVING THE CHARGE FROM C TO A.
Work depends only on the potentials at the two ENDS, since the electrostatic field is conservative — the path along the circumference is irrelevant.
Geometry: B is the centre of the semicircle of radius 5 cm, so both A and C lie 5 cm from B, at opposite ends of the diameter. D lies 10 cm from B along that same line, so
\(CD = 10 - 5 = 5\ \mathrm{cm} \qquad AD = 10 + 5 = 15\ \mathrm{cm}\)
POTENTIAL AT C, from the \(-6\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at B and the \(+6\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at D:
\(V_{C} = \dfrac{k(-6 \times 10^{-6})}{5 \times 10^{-2}} + \dfrac{k(+6 \times 10^{-6})}{5 \times 10^{-2}} = 0\)
The two contributions cancel exactly, because C happens to be equidistant from the two equal and opposite charges.
POTENTIAL AT A, which is 5 cm from B but 15 cm from D:
\(V_{A} = \dfrac{k(-6 \times 10^{-6})}{5 \times 10^{-2}} + \dfrac{k(+6 \times 10^{-6})}{15 \times 10^{-2}}\)
\(V_{A} = k\left(6 \times 10^{-6}\right)\left[\dfrac{1}{0{\cdot}15} - \dfrac{1}{0{\cdot}05}\right] = \left(9 \times 10^{9}\right)\left(6 \times 10^{-6}\right)\left(6{\cdot}67 - 20\right)\)
\(V_{A} = -7{\cdot}2 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}\)
WORK DONE on the \(+5\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) charge:
\(W = q\left(V_{A} - V_{C}\right) = \left(5 \times 10^{-6}\right)\left(-7{\cdot}2 \times 10^{5} - 0\right)\)
\(W = -3{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{J}\)
The work is NEGATIVE, which says the field does the work rather than the external agent: a positive charge moves from C to A of its own accord, being drawn towards the negative charge at B and away from the positive one at D.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem:
(i) A proton moving with velocity \(\vec{V}\) in a non-uniform magnetic field traces a path as shown in the figure.
The path followed by the proton is always in the plane of the paper. What is the direction of the magnetic field in the region near points P, Q and R ? What can you say about relative magnitude of magnetic fields at these points ?
(ii) A current carrying circular loop of area A produces a magnetic field B at its centre. Show that the magnetic moment of the loop is \(\frac{2\mathrm{BA}}{\mu_0}\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{A}}{\pi}}\).
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — sub-part (i) asks for the field direction and the relative field magnitudes at three points that exist only in the drawing. Described: a shaded circle carrying a '+' sign, representing the proton, at the left, with a velocity vector \(\vec{V}\) labelled beside it; from it a path runs to the right, straight at first to a marked point P, then curving through a marked point Q up to a marked point R near the top, and falling away to the right beyond R. Deliberately WITHHELD: the sense in which the path curves at each point and how tightly it is curved there — the first is what fixes the field's direction into or out of the page and the second is what fixes the ordering of the field magnitudes, i.e. both of the things the question asks for. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
(i) DIRECTION AND RELATIVE MAGNITUDE OF THE FIELD.
The force on a moving charge is \(\vec{F} = q\left(\vec{v} \times \vec{B}\right)\), and since the proton curves in the plane of the paper the force is centripetal — directed towards the centre of curvature at each point. The field must be PERPENDICULAR to the plane of the paper, either into it or out of it, and which one is decided by the direction the path bends.
NEAR P, the path curves so that the force points UPWARDS; applying the right-hand rule to \(\vec{v} \times \vec{B}\) for a positive charge, the magnetic field there is INTO the plane of the paper.
NEAR Q, the force again points upwards, so the field there is also INTO the plane of the paper.
NEAR R, the force points DOWNWARDS, so the field there is OUT OF the plane of the paper.
RELATIVE MAGNITUDES. The radius of curvature is
\(r = \dfrac{mv}{qB} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad B \propto \dfrac{1}{r}\)
since m, v and q are the same throughout. So the TIGHTER the curve, the STRONGER the field. Reading the radii off the path: the curvature near R is the sharpest and that near Q the gentlest, so
\(B_{Q} < B_{P} < B_{R}\)
The speed is unchanged along the whole path, which is what makes this reading possible: a magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity and so does no work. Only the DIRECTION of motion changes, never the speed, so every difference in curvature is a difference in field.
(ii) THE MAGNETIC MOMENT OF THE LOOP.
Work back from the two things the question gives — the field at the centre and the area — to the current, and then to the moment.
FROM THE FIELD TO THE CURRENT. At the centre of a circular loop of radius r,
\(B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I}{2r} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad I = \dfrac{2Br}{\mu_{0}}\)
FROM THE AREA TO THE RADIUS:
\(A = \pi r^{2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r = \sqrt{\dfrac{A}{\pi}}\)
THE MAGNETIC MOMENT is the current times the area:
\(M = IA = \left(\dfrac{2Br}{\mu_{0}}\right)A\)
Substituting for r:
\(M = \dfrac{2BA}{\mu_{0}}\sqrt{\dfrac{A}{\pi}}\)
which is the required expression. Notice that M depends on \(A^{3/2}\) — one power of A because the moment is current times area, and a further half power because a larger loop needs MORE current to produce the same field at its centre.

rows.subtopic: Torque on a Current Loop and Magnetic Dipole
rows.stem:
(i) Derive an expression for the torque acting on a rectangular current loop suspended in a uniform magnetic field.
(ii) A charged particle is moving in a circular path with velocity \(\vec{V}\) in a uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\). It is made to pass through a sheet of lead and as a consequence, it looses one half of its kinetic energy without change in its direction. How will (1) the radius of its path (2) its time period of revolution change ?
rows.solution:
(i) TORQUE ON A RECTANGULAR CURRENT LOOP.
Let a rectangular loop of sides a and b, carrying current I, hang in a uniform field \(\vec{B}\), with \(\theta\) the angle between \(\vec{B}\) and the normal \(\hat{n}\) to the loop's plane.
THE FOUR FORCES. Each side feels \(\vec{F} = I\left(\vec{l} \times \vec{B}\right)\).
The two sides of length a lie at an angle to the field; their forces are equal, opposite and ALONG THE SAME LINE, so they cancel completely and produce neither net force nor torque.
The two sides of length b are always PERPENDICULAR to \(\vec{B}\) whatever the loop's orientation, so each carries a force of magnitude
\(\left|\vec{F_{1}}\right| = \left|\vec{F_{2}}\right| = IbB\)
one directed out of the plane of the paper and the other into it. They are equal and opposite but do NOT act along the same line, so they form a COUPLE.
THE TORQUE. The perpendicular distance between the two lines of action is \(a\sin\theta\), so taking moments about the centre,
\(\tau = F_{1}\dfrac{a}{2}\sin\theta + F_{2}\dfrac{a}{2}\sin\theta = (IbB)\,a\sin\theta\)
\(\tau = I(ab)B\sin\theta = IAB\sin\theta\)
where \(A = ab\) is the area. In vector form, with \(\vec{m} = I\vec{A}\),
\(\vec{\tau} = I\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \vec{m} \times \vec{B}\)
The net FORCE is zero while the torque is not, which is what a couple means: the loop rotates without being dragged bodily anywhere. The torque vanishes when \(\theta = 0\), with the loop's normal along the field — the stable position a compass needle settles into, and the position a galvanometer's radial field is designed to prevent the coil ever reaching.
(ii) AFTER THE PARTICLE LOSES HALF ITS KINETIC ENERGY.
(1) THE RADIUS. Express it in terms of the kinetic energy, since that is what the question changes:
\(r = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mK}}{qB} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r \propto \sqrt{K}\)
Halving K therefore gives
\(\dfrac{r'}{r} = \sqrt{\dfrac{K/2}{K}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r' = \dfrac{r}{\sqrt{2}}\)
The radius DECREASES by a factor of \(\sqrt{2}\), to about 71% of its original value — not to half, because the momentum goes as the square root of the energy.
(2) THE TIME PERIOD.
\(T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} = \dfrac{2\pi}{v}\cdot\dfrac{mv}{qB}\)
\(T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}\)
The speed has CANCELLED, so the period does not depend on the kinetic energy at all, and the time period does NOT change.
The two answers together are the fact on which the cyclotron rests: a slower particle travels a smaller circle in exactly the same time, so the period is the same on every orbit and a single fixed-frequency accelerating voltage stays in step with the particle as it spirals outward.

rows.stem:
(i) (1) What are coherent sources ? Why are they necessary for observing a sustained interference pattern ?
(2) Lights from two independent sources are not coherent. Explain.
(ii) Two slits 0.1 mm apart are arranged 1.20 m from a screen. Light of wavelength 600 nm from a distant source is incident on the slits.
(1) How far apart will adjacent bright interference fringes be on the screen ?
(2) Find the angular width (in degree) of the first bright fringe.
rows.solution:
(i) (1) COHERENT SOURCES.
Two sources are coherent if they emit waves of the SAME frequency with a phase difference between them that stays CONSTANT in time — zero or constant, but not varying.
WHY THEY ARE NECESSARY. The intensity at a point where two waves meet is
\(I = I_{1} + I_{2} + 2\sqrt{I_{1}I_{2}}\cos\phi\)
so the position of every bright and dark fringe is fixed by the phase difference \(\phi\) at that point. If \(\phi\) held steady, the pattern stands still and can be seen.
If instead \(\phi\) varied randomly with time, the pattern would shift about far faster than the eye or a detector could follow. Averaging over any observable interval, \(\cos\phi\) averages to ZERO, and
\(I = I_{1} + I_{2}\)
the two intensities simply adding, with no fringes at all — uniform illumination. So a sustained, observable interference pattern requires a constant phase relationship.
(2) WHY TWO INDEPENDENT SOURCES ARE NOT COHERENT.
Light is emitted by individual atoms in short bursts, each lasting only about \(10^{-8}\) s, and the phase of each burst bears no relation to the phase of the last. Within one source this does not matter, because a single source split into two beams sends the SAME burst down both paths, and the phase change affects them equally.
Two INDEPENDENT sources have no such link: their atoms radiate quite independently, so the phase difference between the two beams changes randomly roughly \(10^{8}\) times a second. No steady pattern can survive that, which is why Young's experiment divides ONE beam by a double slit instead of using two separate lamps.
(ii) (1) FRINGE SEPARATION.
The distance between adjacent bright fringes is the fringe width:
\(\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d} = \dfrac{\left(600 \times 10^{-9}\right)\left(1{\cdot}20\right)}{0{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-3}}\)
\(\beta = 7{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m} = 7{\cdot}2\ \mathrm{mm}\)
(2) ANGULAR WIDTH.
\(\theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{d} = \dfrac{600 \times 10^{-9}}{0{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-3}} = 6 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{rad}\)
Converting to degrees, with \(1\ \mathrm{rad} = 57{\cdot}3^{\circ}\):
\(\theta = 6 \times 10^{-3} \times 57{\cdot}3\)
\(\theta \approx 0{\cdot}34^{\circ}\)
The angular width depends only on \(\lambda\) and d, not on D. Moving the screen further away spreads the fringes apart on the screen in exact proportion, but the ANGLES at which the light leaves the slits are unchanged — which is why \(\beta\) grows with D while \(\theta\) does not.

rows.stem:
(i) Define a wavefront. An incident plane wave falls on a convex lens and gets refracted through it. Draw a diagram to show the incident and refracted wavefront.
(ii) A beam of light coming from a distant source is refracted by a spherical glass ball (refractive index 1.5) of radius 15 cm. Draw the ray diagram and obtain the position of the final image formed.
rows.solution:
(i) WAVEFRONT, AND REFRACTION THROUGH A CONVEX LENS.
A WAVEFRONT is the locus of all points of a wave that are oscillating IN PHASE — the surface reached by the disturbance at the same instant. Rays are simply the normals to it.
THE DIAGRAM. Draw a plane wavefront, as a set of straight vertical lines, arriving at a convex lens from the left. On the far side draw the emerging wavefront as a curved arc, CONVERGING towards the focal point F, with its centre of curvature at F. Mark the incident plane wavefront, the refracted spherical wavefront and the focus.
WHY IT CURVES. The lens is THICKEST at its centre and thinnest at its edges, and light travels more slowly in glass than in air. The central part of the wavefront therefore spends the longest time inside the glass and is DELAYED most, while the edges pass through quickly and run ahead. A wavefront that was plane emerges curved, and the shape of the lens is chosen so that the delay varies exactly as needed to make that curve a sphere centred on F.
(ii) REFRACTION THROUGH THE GLASS BALL.
A sphere has two refracting surfaces, so apply the single-surface formula twice, the image from the first acting as the object for the second.
THE RAY DIAGRAM. Draw the ball with centre C, near surface \(P_{1}\) and far surface \(P_{2}\). Show parallel rays arriving from the left, converging inside the glass after refraction at \(P_{1}\), and converging more sharply after refraction at \(P_{2}\) to meet the axis at the final image.
AT THE FIRST SURFACE. Light passes from air into glass, the object is at infinity, and the surface is convex towards the incoming light so \(R = +15\) cm:
\(\dfrac{n_{2}}{v} - \dfrac{n_{1}}{u} = \dfrac{n_{2} - n_{1}}{R}\)
\(\dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{v} - \dfrac{1}{\infty} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}5 - 1}{15} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}5}{15}\)
\(\dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{v} = \dfrac{1}{30} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v = 45\ \mathrm{cm}\)
This first image lies 45 cm beyond \(P_{1}\).
AT THE SECOND SURFACE. The ball has diameter 30 cm, so \(P_{2}\) is 30 cm beyond \(P_{1}\), and the first image lies
\(45 - 30 = 15\ \mathrm{cm}\)
BEYOND \(P_{2}\). The light is converging towards it when it reaches the second surface, so it acts as a VIRTUAL OBJECT at \(u = +15\) cm. Now the light passes from glass into air, and the second surface is convex towards the centre, so \(R = -15\) cm:
\(\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{15} = \dfrac{1 - 1{\cdot}5}{-15} = \dfrac{-0{\cdot}5}{-15} = \dfrac{1}{30}\)
\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{30} + \dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{15} = \dfrac{1}{30} + \dfrac{3}{30} = \dfrac{4}{30}\)
\(v = 7{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{cm}\)
The final image is formed 7.5 cm from the far surface of the ball, on the side away from the incoming light, and it is real.
The virtual object at the second surface is the step that decides the answer: the first image never actually forms, because the second surface intercepts the light before it gets there, and treating that image as a real object 15 cm in FRONT would give the wrong sign and the wrong answer.
